question: what do guests think PMs should do about AI?
answer: There's no single consensus, but several guests converge on becoming a builder. Nikhyl Singhal (nikhyl-singhal-2.md) says PMs whose job was mostly moving information are at risk, and that those who love building will thrive. Tomer Cohen (tomer-cohen.md) describes LinkedIn turning PMs into AI-powered "full stack builders" and putting every PM through an AI academy. Boris Cherny (boris-cherny.md) predicts everyone becomes a product manager and codes. Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) says that with execution cheaper, PMs should lean on influence, judgment and taste. Dan Shipper (dan-shipper-2.md) is "super bullish" on PMs.

question: anyone talk about burnout as a founder or in tech right now?
answer: Yes. Noam Segal (noam-segal.md) discusses the tech worker sentiment survey: burnout is increasing and optimism is declining, and the previous edition was titled "Burnt Out But Optimistic". Molly Graham (molly-graham-2.md) covers grief, loneliness and burnout in tech. Rachel Lockett (rachel-lockett.md) discusses burnout among tech leaders and founders, and says people have more energy when they spend most of their time in their strengths. Simon Willison (simon-willison.md) says running several coding agents at once leaves him exhausted by 11 AM.

question: is it true that software isn't a moat anymore?
answer: Evan Spiegel (evan-spiegel.md) says so directly: "we essentially learned that software is not a moat", and he argues distribution is the new moat. Benedict Evans (benedict-evans.md) is consistent: if the product is a commodity, distribution is what matters. Marc Andreessen (marc-andreessen.md) is more cautious. He says big technology shifts take a long time to play out, and that AI models may end up in an oligopoly or monopoly. The episodes don't claim software has no value, only that it isn't enough of a moat by itself.

question: what do people say about running a bunch of coding agents at once?
answer: Boris Cherny (boris-cherny.md) says he has about five agents running and calls running many Claude sessions in parallel "multi-Claude-ing". Simon Willison (simon-willison.md) can run four in parallel, but says it's mentally exhausting and he's wiped out by 11 AM. He also notes people losing sleep over it. Claire Vo (claire-vo-openclaw.md) runs eight OpenClaw agents. Alexander Embiricos (alexander-embiricos.md) says the bottleneck is validating and reviewing agent code. Tara Seshan (tara-seshan.md) says agent work is mostly one-on-one and hard to share with colleagues. These views differ in emphasis (enthusiasm vs. human limits) rather than flatly disagreeing.

question: do guests think taste still matters when AI can build everything?
answer: Yes, mostly. Adam Mosseri (adam-mosseri.md): "taste matters a ton", because when building is easier, deciding what to build matters more. Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) says humans are still needed to decide what to build and to judge whether it's good ("judgment and taste"), and she adds distribution as a bottleneck. Peter Sellis (peter-sellis.md) ties taste to restraint and saying no. Tony Fadell's episode (tony-fadell.md) is titled around taste, judgment and creativity in the AI era, but I found little direct discussion of taste in the transcript, so coverage there is thin.

question: what's the take on distribution becoming the real moat?
answer: Evan Spiegel (evan-spiegel.md) argues distribution is now the biggest moat and challenge because AI won't help you there, especially for consumer products. Benedict Evans (benedict-evans.md) agrees that if the product is a commodity, distribution matters. Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) calls distribution an underappreciated new bottleneck, since there is so much software competing for attention. Marc Andreessen (marc-andreessen.md) is more cautious about declaring moats this early in a platform shift.

question: anyone talking about AI hardware or glasses or the next form factor?
answer: Yes. Caitlin Kalinowski (caitlin-kalinowski.md) believes AR glasses are part of the future, since looking down at phones is bad for social connection. She worked on Meta's Orion glasses, which she says are ahead of their time: waveguides and microLED aren't yet ready for mass production. Evan Spiegel (evan-spiegel.md) says Snap's Specs come out this year and argues for the next generation of form factors beyond phone screens. Marc Andreessen (marc-andreessen.md) briefly predicts a wearables revolution (pendants, Meta glasses).

question: what should you look at when your product stops growing?
answer: Jason Cohen (jason-cohen.md) gives an ordered diagnostic, saying to fix the first problem you find before the later ones: (1) are customers leaving (logo retention), (2) pricing and positioning, (3) NRR, (4) marketing channels, (5) target market. Elena Verna (elena-verna-40.md) adds that when growth stalls, the biggest opportunity is often the adjacent user just outside your core user.

question: how are people thinking about handing work off as teams scale (and with AI in the mix)?
answer: Molly Graham (molly-graham.md) says as a company scales you should "give away your Legos": hand off what you've gotten good at and move to the next pile, because standing still is the risk. In the AI era (molly-graham-2.md) she adds a caveat: some work shouldn't be outsourced to AI, which she compares to "summer interns", especially things you're individually exceptional at. Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) says humans are still needed on the front end (deciding what to build) and the back end (judgment on whether it's good).

question: anyone talk about replacing sales with AI agents or how GTM changes?
answer: Jeanne Grosser (jeanne-grosser.md) describes Vercel and Stripe examples: a go-to-market engineer builds an agent for a workflow. Vercel's inbound lead agent let 10 SDRs become one human QA-ing the agent, with the other nine moved to outbound. She says humans stay in the loop and that agents will replace the most repetitive prospecting first. Note: Jason Lemkin's episode (jason-m-lemkin.md) is titled about replacing sales with 20 AI agents, but the transcript is about building a human sales team and barely mentions AI, so I can't say what he did with agents.

question: what's the general take — is SaaS doomed?
answer: The transcripts lean no. Dan Shipper (dan-shipper-2.md) calls the "SaaSpocalypse" dumb, says he'd buy SaaS stocks, and expects agents to increase the number of SaaS users. Benedict Evans (benedict-evans.md) says almost no one believes you'll just vibe-code your own Stripe, but that there are open questions about what AI means for the software industry. I didn't find a guest arguing SaaS is doomed, so there's no real disagreement in this set.

question: do guests agree that half of PMs are in trouble?
answer: Only Nikhyl Singhal (nikhyl-singhal-2.md) says it. He estimates about half of product people are "information movers" and that if you don't love building, you're in trouble. Others are related but not the same claim. Dan Shipper (dan-shipper-2.md) is bullish on PMs. Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) asks what a PM's job is if AI does the notes and analysis, and answers influence, judgment and taste. Boris Cherny (boris-cherny.md) expects PM and engineer roles to blur into "builder". So it's one guest's view with partial agreement and some pushback.

question: do people still think lean startup matters in the AI era?
answer: Yes, per Eric Ries himself (eric-ries-2.md). He says people recur with "you don't need lean startup anymore" every wave, and that it's not a religion. The AI labs ship small experiments and research previews and treat things as hypotheses, which he says stands up well. Only this one episode covers it, so coverage is limited to his view.

question: is there consensus that authenticity wins when AI content floods feeds?
answer: Only one guest makes this case. Adam Mosseri (adam-mosseri.md) says AI is a tailwind but also a challenge: with an abundance of synthetic content, people will seek out creativity, authenticity and people, and Instagram should label AI content rather than filter it. Other episodes mention authenticity only in passing, so I can't call it consensus.

question: do guests agree the real AI boom hasn't even started yet?
answer: Mostly Marc Andreessen (marc-andreessen.md) says it. His episode is titled that way and he says we're at the very beginning of several big shifts. Caitlin Kalinowski (caitlin-kalinowski.md) says we're at the beginning of an AI hardware boom, with the physical world as the next frontier. Benedict Evans (benedict-evans.md) is more agnostic: AI is as big as the internet or mobile, but "80 slides of saying we don't know". So it's not a consensus.

question: is influence still the skill AI can't replace or is that just one take?
answer: It's mainly one guest's take. Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) argues influence is the skill AI can't replace, and that PMs should focus on judgment and taste, deciding what to build, and distribution. Others point to different durable skills: Adam Mosseri (adam-mosseri.md) says taste, Molly Graham (molly-graham-2.md) says some work shouldn't be outsourced to AI, and Nikhyl Singhal (nikhyl-singhal-2.md) says builders will thrive. No one else directly argues influence.

question: i heard lovable already hit like a billion in ARR — is that right?
answer: No. Elena Verna (elena-verna-40.md) says Lovable passed $200 million in ARR, in under a year after launch, with fewer than 100 people. The $6 billion figure in the intro is the valuation of its Series B, not ARR.

question: the Claude Code person said only like 10% of their code is AI-written right?
answer: No, the opposite. Boris Cherny (boris-cherny.md), head of Claude Code, says 100% of his code is written by Claude Code and he hasn't edited a line by hand since November.

question: someone said software IS still the moat in the AI era yes?
answer: No. Evan Spiegel (evan-spiegel.md) says "software is not a moat" and that distribution is now the biggest moat. Benedict Evans (benedict-evans.md) says that if the product is a commodity, distribution matters. Nobody in this set says software is still the moat.

question: wasn't it the Snap guy who came up with Proven Better New?
answer: No. Mark Pincus (mark-pincus.md) introduced Proven, Better, New, which he developed at Zynga. Peter Sellis (peter-sellis.md), the first PM at Snapchat, doesn't discuss it.

question: give away your legos is still the unconditional advice in the AI episodes right?
answer: Not quite. In molly-graham.md it was unconditional, i.e. give your Legos away as a company scales. In the AI-era episode (molly-graham-2.md) she says there are Legos that shouldn't be given away, since some work shouldn't be outsourced to AI. She still says to give them away in rapid-scale companies.

question: how should we set OKRs for an AI-native product team?
answer: Coverage is thin. Nothing in these episodes is about OKRs for an AI-native team. Molly Graham (molly-graham.md) is critical of OKR spreadsheets and says goals are a communication tool for clarity, setting goals every two months at seed stage. Eric Ries (eric-ries-2.md) mentions OKRs only as an example of incentives that can undermine principles. I don't know beyond that.

question: how do you run a good board meeting according to these episodes?
answer: I don't know of a board meeting playbook in these episodes. Coverage is limited to passing mentions: Brian Halligan (brian-halligan.md) has a customer panel at HubSpot board meetings, and Keith Rabois (keith-rabois.md) says Roelof Botha praised Square's tempo of shipping fixes between board meetings.

question: how do I get better at influencing execs without just pitching harder?
answer: Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) says to treat executive conversations as discovery, not a pitch. Learn what they care about and how they're measured, and align your idea with their goals. Ask questions like "That's so interesting. What led you to believe that?" Bring real domain expertise rather than being a yes man. Ask for time early, e.g. office hours before you have a one-pager. Match their preferred format and keep detail in the appendix. Bring options, e.g. "what they asked for, plus two more".

question: how do I restart growth when my B2B product stalled?
answer: Jason Cohen (jason-cohen.md) suggests working through his ordered checklist: retention, pricing, NRR, marketing channels, target market. Elena Verna (elena-verna-40.md) adds expanding to the adjacent user just outside your core. The transcripts aren't B2B-specific beyond that.

question: how should I decide what work to keep vs hand off in the AI era?
answer: Molly Graham (molly-graham-2.md) says to hand off most things but keep work where you are individually phenomenal rather than outsourcing it to AI, which she compares to "summer interns". Jessica Fain (jessica-fain.md) says to keep deciding what to build and judging whether it's good (judgment and taste). Adam Mosseri (adam-mosseri.md) says to spend your time on figuring out what to build and be clear-eyed about what AI is good at. Molly Graham's earlier episode (molly-graham.md) still says to give away what you've outgrown.

question: how do I actually use multiple coding agents without losing the plot?
answer: Boris Cherny (boris-cherny.md) says use the most capable model and start most tasks in plan mode, which just tells the model not to write code yet. Simon Willison (simon-willison.md) says four parallel agents wipe him out, so find your limits and don't burn out. Alexander Embiricos (alexander-embiricos.md) says the bottleneck is validation and code review, so configure agents to run tests and validate their own work. Tara Seshan (tara-seshan.md) notes sharing agent threads with colleagues is awkward.

question: how do I repair after a bad meeting with someone on my team?
answer: Dr. Becky Kennedy (dr-becky-kennedy.md) calls repair the number one relationship strategy. Go back, take responsibility for your part, acknowledge the impact, and say what you'll do differently. Her work example: "earlier in the meeting, I totally cut you off. I used a really harsh tone... I'm sorry. I'm going to work on that." She says it re-establishes trust and cooperation. If the other person's behavior was the issue, she suggests addressing it privately and assuming the best of them.
